strengths: Novel and interesting idea: inverting explainability maps at test time to learn a localized embedding token with a fully frozen backbone is a fresh alternative to fine-tuning-based approaches (AlphaCLIP) and input-perturbation approaches (RedCircle, FGVP).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple tasks and datasets (referring expressions on PhraseCut/RefCOCO/RefCOCO+, class retrieval on PascalVOC/PascalContext/COCO/OpenImagesV7, localized captioning), with consistent improvements over reproduced baselines, including strong scaling with backbone size (ViT-H/14 sets SOTA across benchmarks).

Useful technical contributions: gradient decomposition (Sec. 3.3) avoids repeated second-order computations, and the regularization loss provides a tunable local/global trade-off; both are supported by dedicated ablations (Tables 4.5, 5, Appendix E/F).
Good ablation coverage: mask quality (boxes, SAM, erosion/dilation), choice of explainability method, and runtime analysis give insight into the method's behavior and practical applicability.
Adequate documentation of settings, including reproduced baseline results and clear flagging of deviating evaluation protocols, plus appendix details on tasks and limitations.
weaknesses: Inference-time cost is a major practical concern that is under-addressed: MaskInversion requires ~10 gradient descent iterations per mask per image (plus optimization overhead), yet runtime comparisons in Tables 1 and 2 only include accuracy. Against one-forward-pass competitors like AlphaCLIP, the latency/accuracy trade-off on large-scale retrieval is unclear and arguably unfair; the runtime analysis in Table 5 is relegated to an ablation and does not cover larger backbones.

Strong dependence on a single specific explainability method: the ablation (Table 6) shows drastic degradation with GradCAM (34.6) and CheferCAM (12.6) vs. LeGrad (85.4). This fragility limits the claimed generality ('can be used with any differentiable explainability method') and ties the contribution closely to LeGrad (whose authors overlap with this submission).

The localized captioning evaluation protocol is custom-built (matching generated captions to ground-truth referring expressions via CLIP text similarity), which weakens the validity of Table 3; no established benchmark or human evaluation is provided.
Localized diffusion experiments (Sec. 4.4, Figs. 3, 8) are purely qualitative with no quantitative metric, limiting the evidential weight of the third claimed application.

Some clarity and rigor issues: Eq. 6's decomposition is stated rather than formally justified; writing contains multiple typos ('maks', 'Interestringly', 'scall-well', 'sepcifically'); no error bars or variance reporting; sensitivity to K and learning rate only in appendix.

Comparison fairness concerns: several SOTA rows in Table 1 use deviating evaluation settings (region proposals, IoU>0.5 hits), so head-to-head SOTA claims should be softened; some reproduced baselines may be under-tuned.

strengths: The core idea is interesting and somewhat novel: rather than fine-tuning the backbone (AlphaCLIP) or modifying the input image (RedCircle, FGVP, Masked Crop), MaskInversion learns a localized embedding at test time by optimizing an explainability map to match a query mask, keeping the foundation model frozen.

The gradient decomposition (Sec. 3.3) is a clever and well-motivated trick that exploits the fact that the attribution gradient is independent of the query mask, converting a repeated gradient computation into a dot product.

Broad empirical coverage across four tasks (referring expression retrieval, region class retrieval, localized captioning, localized diffusion) and multiple datasets (PhraseCut, RefCOCO/RefCOCO+, PascalVOC, PascalContext, COCO, OpenImagesV7), with unified reproduction of baselines under a shared evaluation setting.
Reasonable ablations: mask quality (Box, Box+SAM, erosion/dilation), choice of explainability method, gradient decomposition runtime, and visualization of the optimization trajectory.
The regularization loss balancing local vs. global context is a sensible design choice, and its task-dependent setting (alpha=0 vs. alpha=5) is explained.
weaknesses: The method depends critically on LeGrad (Bousselham et al., 2024), which appears to be by the same authors; the paper essentially demonstrates that their prior explainability method is the only one that works in this framework (Table 6: LeGrad 85.4 vs. GradCAM 47.6, CheferCAM 12.6). This weakens the generality claim that MaskInversion works with 'any differentiable explainability method' and raises self-promotion/positioning concerns.

Practical cost is not adequately addressed or compared: MaskInversion requires ~10 iterative optimization steps per mask per image at test time, whereas fine-tuned baselines like AlphaCLIP require a single forward pass. The runtime discussion only compares MaskInversion against its own vanilla variant. Overall inference cost relative to baselines is never reported, which is a major omission for a test-time-optimization method.

The localized captioning (Table 3) and diffusion (Sec. 4.4) evaluations are weak: the captioning metric is an ad-hoc, self-constructed protocol (cosine similarity with ground-truth referring expressions, adapted PhraseCut), and the diffusion part is purely qualitative with no quantitative evaluation.

Comparison fairness is questionable: several baselines are evaluated under 'deviating settings' (flagged with ‡), and the authors' reproduced results may not reflect the original methods' intended pipelines, making the SOTA claims less convincing than they appear.

Errors and sloppiness undermine confidence: Table 2 reports Acc@10 = 8.9 for MaskInversion B/32 on PascalVOC (clearly a typo for ~98.9); the text describing Table 6 says MSCOCO but the table reports PascalVOC; multiple typos ('scall-well', 'Interestringly', 'maks', 'sepcifically', 'also significantly AlphaCLIP' missing the verb 'outperforms', 'water and first are in are highly separated').

The claim in Sec. 3.3 that second-order derivatives are avoided is not rigorously verified; no analysis is given of the approximation error introduced by the decomposition, nor of whether the optimization still converges to the same solutions.

Gradient decomposition only provides speedup for >5 masks per image (Table 5); for the common single-mask use case it is actually slower (0.10s vs. 0.13s), which contradicts the framing of it as a general efficiency contribution.

No statistical significance, variance, or hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (K iterations, learning rate) is provided; alpha is tuned per dataset, which raises concerns about generalization to unseen settings.

Novelty is moderate: combining test-time token optimization (textual inversion) with saliency-map supervision (Chefer et al., 2022; Paiss et al., 2022) is an incremental composition rather than a fundamentally new technique.

strengths: The core idea of MaskInversion — inverting a frozen foundation model's explainability map at test time to obtain a localized embedding token — is novel and elegant. It is conceptually distinct from existing visual-prompting methods (RedCircle, FGVP, Masked Crop) and fine-tuning methods (AlphaCLIP), and the analogy to Textual Inversion is well-motivated.

The method requires no fine-tuning of the backbone and works as a drop-in replacement for the CLS token, which is practically attractive and well demonstrated across three different downstream systems (classifier, CLIPCap captioner, diffusion model).

The gradient decomposition trick (Sec. 3.3) is technically sound: since the localized token is independent of the activations, the second-order gradient reduces to a dot product, eliminating repeated backpropagation. The runtime analysis (Table 5, Fig. 6) supports its usefulness for many masks per image.

Breadth of evaluation is a strength: referring expression retrieval (PhraseCut, RefCOCO, RefCOCO+), region-level zero-shot classification (PascalVOC, PascalContext, COCO, OpenImagesV7 with 350 classes), localized captioning, and qualitative diffusion results.

Useful ablations are included: choice of explainability method (Table 6), mask quality (Table 4), regularization loss, number of iterations, and runtime. The limitations section (Appendix H) is honest about dependence on explainability quality and CLIP resolution constraints.
weaknesses: Fairness and comparability of comparisons is a concern. Table 1 mixes 'reported' results under deviating evaluation settings (region proposals, IoU>0.5 hit criterion) with 'reproduced' results under the authors' own protocol. Since the reproduced baselines were adapted to a new setting, some may be disadvantaged (e.g., AlphaCLIP, designed for alpha-mask inputs, underperforms reproduced baselines in ways that are hard to interpret). Claims of 'new SOTA' should be stated more cautiously.

Anomalies and apparent errors in the tables undermine confidence: Table 2 reports Acc@10 = 8.9 for B/32 on PascalVOC (obviously a typo), an odd '71.61' for B/16 on COCO, and Table 6 states results 'on the MSCOCO dataset' while the table caption says PascalVOC. These need fixing.

The localized captioning evaluation protocol is entirely self-designed (caption judged correct if its CLIP text-embedding similarity to a ground-truth referring expression is highest among candidates in the image). No standard captioning metrics or human evaluation are provided, so Table 3 evidence is weak; also CLIPCap is trained against vanilla CLIP features, so the drop-in replacement assumption deserves more justification.
The diffusion experiments (Sec. 4.4) are purely qualitative with no quantitative protocol, making the 'localized diffusion' application more of a showcase than a validated capability.

Per-mask test-time optimization is a significant practical cost: every query mask on every image requires ~10 gradient iterations, and the runtime gain from decomposition is modest for small numbers of masks (Table 5). A thorough cost/benefit discussion versus simply running the model once per crop, or versus training-free baselines, is missing.

Writing quality is below bar for a top venue: typos and broken sentences throughout ('sepcifically', 'Interestringly', 'scall-well', 'the learned can be used', 'also significantly AlphaCLIP', 'first are in are highly separated'), and the project page URL is empty.

Circularity/dependency risk: the method's headline performance relies heavily on LeGrad (Table 6 shows a huge gap: 85.4 vs 47.6 for GradCAM‡), and LeGrad's authors overlap with this submission; the paper should discuss generalization to other attribution methods and backbones (only CLIP-family models are tested, despite claims of generality to 'any pre-trained model').

strengths: Novel and elegant core idea: learning a mask-localized embedding at test time by optimizing an embedding token so that its explainability map matches the query mask, requiring no modification or fine-tuning of the frozen backbone — a genuinely different approach from visual prompt engineering (RedCircle, FGVP, Masked Crop) and mask-conditioned pretraining (AlphaCLIP).

Broad and thorough empirical evaluation across four distinct downstream tasks (referring expression retrieval, zero-shot region class retrieval, localized captioning, localized image generation) and six datasets (PascalVOC, PascalContext, COCO, PhraseCut, RefCOCO/RefCOCO+, OpenImagesV7), with consistent improvements over strong baselines and clear scaling behavior across ViT-B/32 to ViT-H/14.

The gradient decomposition trick is well motivated and the appendix provides a formal, correct derivation of the exactness of the decomposition; runtime experiments (Tables 5, 10; Figure 6) quantify the speedup and show favorable scaling with resolution and number of masks.

Extensive ablations: sensitivity to mask quality (erosion/dilation/boxes/SAM), number of iterations with a convergence analysis justifying K=10, the regularization hyperparameter α with qualitative and quantitative analysis, and dependence on the choice of explainability method.

Honest discussion of limitations (dependence on the quality of the explainability method, CLIP's low input resolution) and comparison against recent training-free methods (MaskCLIP, CLIPSurgery, SCLIP) with larger gaps at bigger model scales.
weaknesses: The performance margin over the simple Masked Crop baseline is modest on some tasks (e.g., ~3-4 points on RefCOCO/RefCOCO+ at ViT-B/16), while MaskInversion requires per-mask test-time optimization (10 gradient descent steps plus backpropagation); a latency/accuracy trade-off comparison against Masked Crop (which is essentially free at inference) would strengthen the practical case for the method.

Baseline comparisons are complicated by mixed evaluation protocols: reported numbers from prior works use deviating settings (region proposals, IoU>0.5 hits), and many key baselines are 'reproduced' under an adapted protocol; although the authors are transparent about this, direct comparability of Table 1 numbers across the ‡ and ∗ groups remains limited.

The method exhibits strong sensitivity to the choice of explainability method (Table 8: 85.4 with LeGrad vs. 12.6 with CheferCAM vs. 47.6 with modified GradCAM), suggesting the contribution partly rests on the properties of one specific attribution method; the paper would benefit from more analysis of why the optimization is so fragile across attribution methods and any guidance or robustness mitigations.

The localized captioning evaluation protocol is somewhat ad hoc: no standard dataset or metric exists, captions are judged correct via CLIP-text similarity ranking against ground-truth referring expressions, which is an indirect proxy whose correlation with caption quality is not validated.

Hyperparameter treatment raises mild tuning concerns: α is set to 5 for RefCOCO/RefCOCO+ but 0 for all other datasets, which appears dataset-specific and is chosen using downstream accuracy; a justification for how this transfers to unseen datasets is missing, and no statement about code release is provided.

The theoretical understanding of why optimizing an explainability map yields a semantically faithful region embedding (rather than merely an attention-localizing token) is largely empirical; a deeper analysis or discussion of potential failure modes (e.g., tokens that localize attention but encode wrong semantics) would improve the paper.

strengths: The core idea of using a differentiable explainability map as an optimization objective to learn a test-time localized embedding token is interesting and distinct from input-prompting (RedCircle, FGVP, Masked Crop) and mask-conditioned finetuning (AlphaCLIP) approaches.
The method requires no backbone modification or fine-tuning and works as a drop-in replacement for the CLS token, which is practically appealing.

Broad empirical evaluation across multiple tasks (referring expression retrieval, class retrieval, localized captioning, diffusion) and datasets (PhraseCut, RefCOCO/RefCOCO+, PascalVOC, PascalContext, COCO, OpenImagesV7), with consistent improvements over reproduced baselines and training-free methods (MaskCLIP, CLIPSurgery, SCLIP).

The gradient decomposition trick is well motivated and the appendix provides a correct, formally written proof of its exactness; runtime ablations (Table 5, Fig. 10) and convergence analysis (Fig. 5) support the design choices.
The paper includes a reasonable set of ablations: mask quality/degradation, choice of explainability method, regularization weight α, number of iterations, and multi-mask scalability.
weaknesses: Strong dependence on a specific explainability method: the LeGrad ablation (Table 8) shows a very large gap (85.4 vs. 47.6 for GradCAM‡ and 12.6 for CheferCAM), meaning the reported results largely reflect the quality of LeGrad rather than a general property of the inversion framework; the generality claim ('works with any differentiable explainability method') is not well supported.

Test-time optimization per mask adds non-trivial inference cost and complexity relative to simple training-free baselines, and the practical benefit over the strong Masked Crop baseline is moderate on several settings (e.g., RefCOCO/RefCOCO+ reproduced baselines), making the overall significance questionable.

The evaluation protocol is largely self-constructed (ground-truth masks with a custom retrieval setup, an adapted PhraseCut captioning metric based on CLIP text-encoder similarity), and comparisons to prior work mix 'as-reported' numbers from deviating settings with reproduced numbers, weakening direct comparability of the SOTA claims.

Novelty is incremental: test-time prompt/token optimization and explainability-guided training (Chefer et al. 2022, Paiss et al. 2022) already exist; the main contributions (Dice-loss-guided token inversion and a gradient decomposition shortcut) are relatively straightforward combinations of known components.

Computational cost comparisons are limited: the paper reports runtime for the decomposition but does not report wall-clock comparison or accuracy-vs-cost trade-offs against cheaper baselines such as Masked Crop, which requires a single forward pass.

Per-dataset hyperparameter choices (α=5 only for RefCOCO/RefCOCO+, 0 elsewhere) and evaluation at interpolated 448×448 resolution complicate reproducibility and suggest sensitivity to setup; the ablations are in the appendix and somewhat fragmented.

The localized captioning evaluation (top-1 CLIP-similarity retrieval against referring expressions) is a weak proxy for caption quality and could favor embeddings aligned with the CLIP text space by construction.

strengths: Novel and elegant idea: learning a localized embedding at test time by optimizing a token so that its explainability map matches a query mask, requiring no modification or fine-tuning of the frozen foundation model — a genuinely distinct direction from input-perturbation (RedCircle, FGVP, Masked Crop) and fine-tuning approaches (AlphaCLIP, CPT).

Broad and convincing empirical evaluation: four downstream task families (referring expression retrieval, zero-shot region class retrieval, localized captioning, localized diffusion) across many datasets (PascalVOC, PascalContext, COCO, PhraseCut, RefCOCO/RefCOCO+, OpenImagesV7), with consistent SOTA results and clear scaling behavior across CLIP backbones (B/32 to H/14).

The gradient decomposition (Eq. 5) is well motivated and mathematically exact (a clean derivation is provided in Appendix I.1), yielding practical speedups for multi-mask images and improved numerical stability by avoiding repeated second-order backpropagation.

Thorough ablation studies: mask quality (erosion/dilation/boxes/Box+SAM), choice of explainability method, number of iterations K, hyperparameter α for local/global trade-off, and runtime scalability with resolution and token count.
Comparison against training-free region-pooling methods (MaskCLIP, CLIPSurgery, SCLIP) is valuable and shows that the advantage grows with backbone size, a practically relevant finding.
weaknesses: Test-time cost: MaskInversion requires a per-image forward pass plus K gradient descent iterations per query mask (second-order-free, but still iterative optimization), making it substantially more expensive than pure training-free baselines (MaskCLIP, CLIPSurgery, SCLIP) at inference; the runtime comparison is only against the vanilla variant of the method itself, not against baselines.

Heavy dependence on the choice of explainability method (LeGrad gives 85.4 vs. GradCAM 34.6 on PascalVOC, Table 8) is a significant fragility. Since LeGrad is a very recent method (Bousselham et al., 2025) plausibly from the same group, the paper effectively relies on its own attribution method; generality to other backbones with weaker explainability methods is not demonstrated.

Potential circularity/evaluation concerns: the token is optimized to maximize explainability-map alignment, and several qualitative analyses (Fig. 3, 12) validate the method via the same explainability maps, which risks self-confirmation. The localized captioning metric (top-1 retrieval of ground-truth referring expressions via CLIP text similarity) is non-standard and could favor embeddings that align with CLIP's text space.

Baseline comparisons require adapted reproduction settings (marked ∗/‡) because original evaluation protocols differ; some reported reproduced numbers differ noticeably from original papers, and the fairness of the ground-truth-mask protocol for baselines like ReCLIP/FGVP (designed with region proposals) could be debated.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: α must be tuned per dataset (5 for RefCOCO/RefCOCO+, 0 elsewhere), and the catastrophic drop at α = 20 (20.5% accuracy) suggests the method is sensitive to configuration; no principled selection procedure is given.

Per-mask independent optimization means embeddings for multiple masks of the same image are computed separately, which may limit efficiency in dense-scene applications despite the decomposition trick; also, resolution was silently raised from 224 to 448 via positional embedding interpolation, which is only mentioned in the limitations appendix and complicates reproduction/comparability.
